॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

वी॒रस्य॒ नु स्वश्वं॑ जनासः॒ प्र नु वो॑चाम वि॒दुर॑स्य दे॒वाः ।
षो॒ह्ना यु॒क्ताः पंच॑पं॒चा व॑हंति म॒हद्दे॒वाना॑मसुर॒त्व ॑ मेकं ॥ १८ ॥

vīrasya nu svaśvaṃ janāsaḥ pra nu vocāma vidurasya devāḥ |
ṣohnā yuktāḥ paṃcapaṃcā vahaṃti mahaddevānāmasuratva
mekaṃ ‖ 18 ‖

॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

वीरस्य । नु । सुअश्वं । जनासः । प्र । नु । वोचाम । विदुः । अस्य : देवाः ।
षोह्ना । युक्ताः । पंचपंच । आ । वहंति । महत् । देवानां । असुरत्वं । एकं॥

vīrasya | nu | suaśvaṃ | janāsaḥ | pra | nu | vocāma | viduḥ | asya : devāḥ |
ṣohnā | yuktāḥ | paṃcapaṃca | ā | vahaṃti | mahat | devānāṃ | asuratvaṃ | ekaṃ‖

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

हे जनासो जना वीरस्य शूरस्येंद्रस्य स्वश्वं शोभनाश्वेपेतत्वं नु क्षिप्रं प्र वोचाम । प्रकर्षण वदाम । तथा देवा अप्यस्येंद्रस्य स्वश्वतं विदुः । जानंति । किं तत्स्वश्वत्वं । तदुच्यते । षोळ्ता मासानां द्वंद्वयोगकाले षोढा दृश्यमाना ऋतवोऽश्वा निरूप्यंते । ते च षट्संख्याका ऋतवॊः हेमंततिशिरयोः समासेन पंच पंच युक्ताः संतः कालात्मकमिंद्रमा वहंति । तदिदमि-द्रस्य स्वश्वत्वं यद्वृतुभिरूढत्वं ॥ षोळ्ता । षष्‌शब्दात्संख्याया विधार्थे धेति धाप्रत्ययः ' षष उत्वं दतृदशधासूत्तरपदादेः ष्टुत्वं च । पा ६-३-१०९-३ इत्युत्वं ष्टुत्वं च।प्रत्ययस्वरः॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

"O people, let us quickly proclaim the good-horsedness (स्वश्वं (svaśvaṃ)) of the hero, the brave Indra, that is, his being possessed of fine horses; and the gods too know his good-horsedness." What is that good-horsedness? It is explained: षोळ्हा (ṣoḷhā), at the time of the pairing of the months, the seasons seen as sixfold are represented as horses. Those seasons, six in number, with Hemanta and Śiśira taken together, are yoked five and five and carry Indra, who is of the nature of time. This is Indra's good-horsedness, that he is carried by the seasons. (The rest of the block is grammar.)

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • जनासः (janāsaḥ)—O people
  • वीरस्य (vīrasya)—of the brave Indra
  • स्वश्वं (svaśvaṃ)—the being accompanied by horses
  • नु (nu)—right now
  • प्र वोचाम (pra vocāma)—we proclaim and praise
  • देवाः (devāḥ)—the gods also
  • अस्य (asya)—this Indra's being yoked with horses
  • नु (nu)—at once
  • विदुः (viduḥ)—know
  • षोळ्हा (ṣoḷhā)—the horses in the form of the six seasons
  • पंचपंचयुक्ताः (paṃcapaṃcayuktāḥ)—(Hemanta and Śiśira being undivided) five

p. 312

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • आ वहंति (ā vahaṃti)—carry Indra
  • देवानां (devānāṃ)—of the gods
  • असुरत्वं (asuratvaṃ)—the might
  • महत् (mahat)—great
  • एकं (ekaṃ)—unique (one without a second)
भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

People, we proclaim and praise the fact that Indra, the hero, is endowed with horses. The gods too know that Indra is endowed with horses. The horses, which are of the nature of time as the six seasons, are five in form through the union of the seasons Hemanta and Śiśira, and they carry Indra. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

English translation (H. H. Wilson)

We proclaim, people, the wealth of the hero, (Indra), in horses ; the gods know his (affluence) ; six, or five and five, harnessed to his car, convey him ; great and unequalled is the might of the gods,

विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

षोळ्ता (ṣoḷtā)—मासानां द्वंद्वयोगकाले षोढा दृश्यमानाः ऋतवः अश्वाः निरूप्यंते । (māsānāṃ dvaṃdvayogakāle ṣoḍhā dṛśyamānāḥ ṛtavaḥ aśvāḥ nirūpyaṃte |) । ते च षट् संख्याकाः (te ca ṣaṭ saṃkhyākāḥ) । ऋतवः हेमंतशिशिरयोः समासेन पंचपंच युक्ताः संतः कालात्मकमिंद्रं आवहंति । (ṛtavaḥ hemaṃtaśiśirayoḥ samāsena paṃcapaṃca yuktāḥ saṃtaḥ kālātmakamiṃdraṃ āvahaṃti |) । तदिदं इंद्रस्य स्वश्वत्वं यदृतभिरूढत्वं (tadidaṃ iṃdrasya svaśvatvaṃ yadṛtabhirūḍhatvaṃ) । It is described that Indra is endowed with excellent horses, and that the gods too know this endowment of Indra with excellent horses: अस्य स्वश्वत्वं देवा आपि जानंति (asya svaśvatvaṃ devā āpi jānaṃti). The endowment with excellent horses stated here is explained by the exposition "ṣoḷhā". Indra is of the form of time; for Indra, who is of the nature of time, the twelve months combine into six pairs of seasons. Of these, if the two seasons Hemanta and Śiśira join as one, there are five seasons. Thus these seasons, five in number, are represented as five horses; these five horses carry Indra, who is of the form of time. This is what is meant by Indra's being endowed with excellent horses through the seasons. Although six seasons arise from twelve months, Hemanta and Śiśira, being possessed of one and the same kind of quality, are reckoned as one. Thus the five seasons are five horses, and they carry Indra, who is time-natured through identity with the sun; and the greatness of Indra is described as mighty. वीरो वीरयत्यमित्रान् वेतेर्वा स्याद्गतिकर्मणः वीरयेतेर्वा (vīro vīrayatyamitrān vetervā syādgatikarmaṇaḥ vīrayetervā) (Ni. 1-7). Yāska explains the word vīra thus: one who destroys enemies in many ways, who goes to face the enemies and confronts them, who is endowed with valour.

p. 313

Ṛk 19

॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

देवत्वष्टा सविता विश्वरूपः पुपोष प्रजाः पुरुधा जजान।
इमा च विश्वा भुवनान्यस्य महद्देवानामसुरत्वमेकं ॥१९॥

devatvaṣṭā savitā viśvarūpaḥ pupoṣa prajāḥ purudhā jajāna|
imā ca viśvā bhuvanānyasya mahaddevānāmasuratvamekaṃ ‖19‖

॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

देव । त्वष्टा । सविता । विश्वरूपः । पुपोष । प्रजाः । पुरुधा । जजान ।
इमा । च । विश्वा । भुवनानि । अस्य । महत् । देवानां । असुरत्वं । एकं ॥ १९ ॥

deva | tvaṣṭā | savitā | viśvarūpaḥ | pupoṣa | prajāḥ | purudhā | jajāna |
imā | ca | viśvā | bhuvanāni | asya | mahat | devānāṃ | asuratvaṃ | ekaṃ ‖ 19 ‖

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

त्वाष्टे पशौ हविषोऽनुवाक्या देवस्त त्वष्टेतेषा । सूत्रितं च । देवस्त त्वष्टा सविता विश्वरूपो देव त्वष्टर्यद्ध चारुत्वमानट् । आ. ३-८ । इति ॥ सवितांतर्यामितया सर्वस्य प्रेरको विश्वरूपो नानाविधरूपस्त्वष्टा त्वष्टनामको देवः प्रजाः पुरुधा बहुधा जजान । जनयति । ताश्च पुपोष । पोषयति । इमेमानि विश्वा विश्वानि सर्वाणि भुवनानि भूतजातानि चास्य त्वष्टुः संबंधीनि ॥ विश्वरूपः । बहुव्रीहौ विश्वं संज्ञायामिति पूर्वपदांतोदात्तत्वं ॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

The verse is the anuvākyā for the oblation in the Tvāṣṭra animal sacrifice, the verse देवस्त त्वष्टेतेषा (devasta tvaṣṭeteṣā); and it is prescribed in the sūtra (Ā. Sū. 3-8).NOTE Savitā is the impeller of all as the inner controller; Tvaṣṭṛ, the god so named, of many kinds of form (viśvarūpa), begets the creatures in many ways (purudhā) and nourishes them. All these worlds, all the beings, belong to this Tvaṣṭṛ.

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • सविता (savitā)—the impeller of all
  • विश्वरूपः (viśvarūpaḥ)—the one with many kinds of form
  • त्वष्टा देवः (tvaṣṭā devaḥ)—Tvaṣṭṛ, who is of divine nature
  • प्रजाः (prajāḥ)—the creatures
  • पुरुधा (purudhā)—in many ways
  • जजान (jajāna)—creates
  • पुपोष (pupoṣa)—(and) nourishes
  • इमा विश्वा भुवनानि (imā viśvā bhuvanāni)—all these beings, all of them
  • अस्य (asya)—belong to this Tvaṣṭṛ
  • देवानां (devānāṃ)—of the gods
  • असुरत्वं (asuratvaṃ)—the might
  • महत् (mahat)—great
  • एकं (ekaṃ)—extraordinary
भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Tvaṣṭṛ, the impeller of all, of many kinds of form, of divine nature, creates the creatures in many ways and nourishes them. All these beings too belong to that Tvaṣṭṛ. The might of the gods is great and extraordinary.

English translation (H. H. Wilson)

The divine Twashtri the impeller (of all), the multiform, has begotten and nourished a numerous progeny, for all these worlds are of him : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

p. 314

विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

सविता (savitā)—अंतर्यामितया सर्वस्य प्रेरकः (aṃtaryāmitayā sarvasya prerakaḥ) । Sāyaṇa explains that the word savitṛ means "one who impels everything, since he is the inner controller". Yāska explains: सविता सर्वस्य प्रसविता (savitā sarvasya prasavitā)—Savitā is the one who brings forth everything. त्वष्टा देवः प्रजाः पुरुधा जजान पुपोष विश्वा भुवनानि च अस्य (tvaṣṭā devaḥ prajāḥ purudhā jajāna pupoṣa viśvā bhuvanāni ca asya)—तृष्णनामकः देवः प्रजाः बहुधा जनयति पोषयति (tṛṣṇanāmakaḥ devaḥ prajāḥ bahudhā janayati poṣayati) । इमानि सर्वाणि भूतजातानि च त्वष्टुः संबंधीनि (imāni sarvāṇi bhūtajātāni ca tvaṣṭuḥ saṃbaṃdhīni) । Sāyaṇa states that the god named Tvaṣṭṛ has fashioned the creatures in many ways and nourishes them, and that all these creatures belong to the god Tvaṣṭṛ. Yāska gives the etymology of this Ṛk as follows: देवस्त्वष्टा सविता सर्वरूपः पोषति प्रजाः रसानुप्रदादेन बहुधा चेमा जनयतीमानि च सर्वाणि भूतान्वयदकान्यस्य महच्चास्मै देवानामसुरत्वमेकं प्रज्ञावत्त्वं वानवत्त्वं नापि ना । (devastvaṣṭā savitā sarvarūpaḥ poṣati prajāḥ rasānupradādena bahudhā cemā janayatīmāni ca sarvāṇi bhūtānvayadakānyasya mahaccāsmai devānāmasuratvamekaṃ prajñāvattvaṃ vānavattvaṃ nāpi nā |) । असुरिति प्रज्ञानाम अस्यत्यनर्थान् अस्ताश्चास्यामर्थाः (asuriti prajñānāma asyatyanarthān astāścāsyāmarthāḥ) । असुरत्वमादिलुप्तं (asuratvamādiluptaṃ) । (Ni. 10-34) The god Tvaṣṭṛ has brought all creatures into being. By bestowing waters he nourishes and increases them. These beings and the waters belong to this god; therefore this god produces the creatures, nourishes and increases them. Hence the asuratva of this god is explained as extraordinary. He also explains the meaning of the word asura: because it averts dangers, nothing is expressible by the word asu as "intelligence", or falls outside the range of intelligence; therefore asura is said to mean "possessed of intelligence".NOTE And: असुरत्वं वसुमतो भावः वसुरत्वं (asuratvaṃ vasumato bhāvaḥ vasuratvaṃ) । रः मत्त्वर्थे वकारलोपश्च (raḥ mattvarthe vakāralopaśca) वसुना उदकेन तद्वान् असौ त्वष्टा (vasunā udakena tadvān asau tvaṣṭā) । He explains that the word asuratva is used for vasuratva, that here "ra" is used in the sense of "possessing" and that "va" is dropped, and he gives another meaning: वसुना उदकेन तद्वान् (vasunā udakena tadvān)—one who is endowed with waters. Durgācārya comments: तया महत्या प्रज्ञया उदकेन साधनेन सर्वमिदं जनयति पुष्णाति वर्धयति च । (tayā mahatyā prajñayā udakena sādhanena sarvamidaṃ janayati puṣṇāti vardhayati ca |)—being possessed of abundant intelligence, the god Tvaṣṭṛ produces everything by means of the waters, nourishes it and increases it. In the second explanation given by him: असुरत्वं अन्नवत्त्वं (asuratvaṃ annavattvaṃ) । असुः प्राणः तेन तद्वत्वं (asuḥ prāṇaḥ tena tadvatvaṃ)—asuratva is the state of being endowed with breath; अन्नवत्त्वं तेषामन्नहेतुनोदकेन तद्वत्वं (annavattvaṃ teṣāmannahetunodakena tadvatvaṃ)—he is endowed with the waters that are the cause of food for the creatures.

p. 315

In Sāyaṇa's explanation, विश्वा भुवनानि (viśvā bhuvanāni) is given the meaning सर्वाणि भूतजातानि (sarvāṇi bhūtajātāni)—the totality of creatures of many kinds. In the Nirukta commentators' explanation, सर्वाणि भूतानि उदकानि (sarvāṇi bhūtāni udakāni)—he makes all creatures and the waters, nourishes and increases them; thus a difference can be seen. A difference is also seen in the explanation of the meaning of the word asuratva.

Ṛk 20

॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

मही समैरच्चम्वा समीची उभे ते अस्य वसुना नृष्टे ।
शृण्वे वीरो विंदमानो वसूनि महद्देवानामसुरत्वमेकं ॥ २० ॥

mahī samairaccamvā samīcī ubhe te asya vasunā nṛṣṭe |
śṛṇve vīro viṃdamāno vasūni mahaddevānāmasuratvamekaṃ ‖ 20 ‖

॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

मही इति । सम् । ऐरत् । चम्या । समीची इति सम्ईची । उभे इति । ते इति ।
अस्य । वसुना । नृष्टे इति निऋष्टे ।
शृण्वे । वीरः । विंदमानः । वसूनि । महत् । देवानां । असुरत्वं । एकं ॥ २० ॥

mahī iti | sam | airat | camyā | samīcī iti samīcī | ubhe iti | te iti |
asya | vasunā | nṛṣṭe iti niṛṣṭe |
śṛṇve | vīraḥ | viṃdamānaḥ | vasūni | mahat | devānāṃ | asuratvaṃ | ekaṃ ‖ 20 ‖

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

मही महत्वा समीचि परस्परं संगते चम्वा चमंत्यदंत्यनयोर्देवमनुष्या इति चम्वौ । यद्वा चम्येते आद्येते भूतजातैरिति चम्वौ द्यावापृथिव्यौ । समैरत् । इंद्रः प्रजापश्वादिभिः सम्यगयोजयत् । ते उभे द्यावापृथिव्यावस्येंद्रस्य वसुना तेजसा धनेन वा नृष्टे निकरां व्याप्ते भवतः।वीरः समर्थः स इंद्रो वसूनि शत्रूनभिभूय तदीयानि धनानि विंदमानो लभमानः सन् श्वण्वे । सर्वैः श्रूयते । तवेदिदमभितश्चेकिते वसु। ऋग्वे. १-५३-३ । इत्यादिषु दृष्टत्वात् ॥ ऐरत्। ईर गतावित्यस्य लजि रूपं । नृष्टे । ऋषी गतौ । कर्मणि क्तः । गतिरनंतर इति गतेः स्वरः । शृण्वे । श्रु श्रवण इत्यस्य व्यत्ययेन कर्मणि श्नुः । लोपस्त आत्मनेपदेष्टिति तलोपः । विंदमानः । विद्ल लाभ इत्यस्य लटि शानचि रूपं । तस्य लसार्वधातुकस्वरे धातुस्वरः ॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

चम्वा (camvā) (dual) are the two that are "chewed", for in them gods and men eat (चमंत्यदंत्यनयोर्देवमनुष्या इति (camaṃtyadaṃtyanayordevamanuṣyā iti)); or else they are the two that are eaten by the creatures—heaven and earth. "Mahī" means great, "samīcī" mutually joined. समैरत् (samairat): Indra joined them well with creatures, animals and the rest. Both heaven and earth are pervaded by this Indra's वसुना (vasunā)—by his splendour or by his wealth. वीरः (vīraḥ) means capable. That Indra, overcoming his enemies and obtaining their wealth (वसूनि (vasūni)), is heard of by all; for this is seen in such passages as तवेदिदमभितश्चेकिते वसु (tavedidamabhitaścekite vasu) (Ṛgve. 1-53-3).NOTE

p. 316

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • मही (mahī)—those of great nature
  • समीची (samīcī)—and joined together
  • चम्वा (camvā)—heaven and earth
  • सम्मैरत् (sammairat)—(Indra) made them endowed with creatures
  • ते उभे (te ubhe)—both of them, heaven and earth
  • अस्य (asya)—of Indra
  • वसुना (vasunā)—by the splendour
  • नृष्टे (nṛṣṭe)—are pervaded
  • वीरः (vīraḥ)—the capable Indra
  • वसूनि (vasūni)—the wealth of enemies
  • विंदमानः (viṃdamānaḥ)—as one who seizes
  • शृण्वे (śṛṇve)—is heard of as well known
  • देवानां (devānāṃ)—of the gods
  • असुरत्वं (asuratvaṃ)—the might
  • महत् (mahat)—great
  • एकं (ekaṃ)—unique
भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Indra made heaven and earth, which are of great nature and joined together, endowed with creatures. Both heaven and earth are pervaded by Indra's splendour. It is well known that Indra, the capable, seizes the wealth of enemies. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

English translation (H. H. Wilson)

He has filled the two vast receptacles (heaven and earth) united (with creatures): they are both penetrated by his lustre: the hero spoiling the treasures (of the foe) is renowned : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

चम्वा (camvā)—चमंति अदंति अनयोः देवमनुष्याः इति चम्वा (camaṃti adaṃti anayoḥ devamanuṣyāḥ iti camvā) । यद्वा चम्येते अद्येते भूतजात्यैरिति चम्वा द्यावापृथिव्यौ । (yadvā camyete adyete bhūtajātyairiti camvā dyāvāpṛthivyau |) । The word chamvā is stated among the names of heaven and earth (Ni. 3-22). Since they are the cause of the production of food fit to be eaten by gods and men, and since they are consumed by all creatures, heaven and earth are designated by the word chamvā. वसुना (vasunā)—तेजसा धनेन वा (tejasā dhanena vā) । The word vasu is stated among the names of rays (Ni. 2-15) and among the names of wealth (Ni. 3-9); and in सुगुर सत्सुहिरण्यः (sugura satsuhiraṇyaḥ) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-1-18) it is used in the sense वसुना अन्नेन (vasunā annena)—"with food". And it is also explained: वसवः आदित्यरश्मयः (vasavaḥ ādityaraśmayaḥ) (Ni. 12-42)—the rays of the sun. Here it is described that heaven and earth are pervaded by Indra's splendours and wealth, pervaded by Indra's lordliness.

p. 317

वीरः वसूनि विंदमानः शृण्वे (vīraḥ vasūni viṃdamānaḥ śṛṇve)—समर्थः सः इंद्रः शत्रूनभिभूय तदीयानि धनानि लभमानस्सर् (samarthaḥ saḥ iṃdraḥ śatrūnabhibhūya tadīyāni dhanāni labhamānassar) सर्वैः श्रूयते (sarvaiḥ śrūyate)NOTE—having explained that the heroic Indra subdues his enemies and seizes their wealth, he describes that this matter is stated in the Ṛk तवेदिदमभितश्चेकिते वसु (tavedidamabhitaścekite vasu) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-53-3).

Ṛk 21

॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

इमां च नः पृथिवीं विश्वधायाउप क्षेति हितमित्रो न राजा।

imāṃ ca naḥ pṛthivīṃ viśvadhāyāupa kṣeti hitamitro na rājā|

॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

इमां । च । नः । पृथिवीं । विश्वधायाः । उप । क्षेति । हितमित्रः ! न ! राजा ।
पुरःसदः । शर्मसदः । न । वीराः । महत् । देवानां । असुरत्वं । एकं ॥ २१ ॥

imāṃ | ca | naḥ | pṛthivīṃ | viśvadhāyāḥ | upa | kṣeti | hitamitraḥ ! na ! rājā |
puraḥsadaḥ | śarmasadaḥ | na | vīrāḥ | mahat | devānāṃ | asuratvaṃ | ekaṃ ‖ 21 ‖

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

विश्वधाया विश्वस्य धाता सर्वान्नो ना नोऽस्माकं राजेंद्र इमां पृथिवीमंतरिक्षं चोप तयोः समीपे क्षेति । निवसति । तत्र दृष्टांतः । हितमित्रो न । यथा कस्यचित् हितोपदेष्टा सुहृत्समीपे निवसति तद्वत् । वीराः समर्था युद्धसहाया मरुतः पुरःसदो युद्धार्थं पुरतो निश्चयेन गंतार इंद्रस्य शर्मसदः । न चार्थे । शर्मणि गृहे सीदंतश्च भवंति । यत्र यत्रासौ तत्र तत्र संनिधिं कुर्वाणा इत्यर्थः ॥ क्षेति । क्षि निवासगत्योरित्यस्य लटि बहुलं छंदसीति विकरणस्य लुक् । निघातः ॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

विश्वधायाः (viśvadhāyāḥ) is the supporter of all. Our king Indra dwells near this earth and the atmosphere, close to them. The illustration: हितमित्रो न (hitamitro na)—as a friend who gives beneficial counsel dwells near one's side. The वीराः (vīrāḥ) are the capable Maruts, helpers in battle, पुरःसदः (puraḥsadaḥ)—those who go resolutely before Indra for battle; शर्मसदः (śarmasadaḥ)—here न (na) is in the sense of "and" (न चार्थे (na cārthe)): they are also seated in his house (śarman); the meaning is that wherever he is, there they keep close at hand.

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • विश्वधायाः (viśvadhāyāḥ)—the supporter of the whole world
  • नः (naḥ)—to us
  • राजा (rājā)—the lord, Indra
  • हितमित्रो न (hitamitro na)—like a friend who wishes one well
  • इमां पृथिवीं उप (imāṃ pṛthivīṃ upa)—in the atmosphere near this earth
  • क्षेति (kṣeti)—dwells
  • वीराः (vīrāḥ)—the capable Maruts
  • पुरःसदः (puraḥsadaḥ)—going in front of him (in battle)
  • शर्मसदः (śarmasadaḥ)—dwell in his very house
  • देवानां (devānāṃ)—of the gods
  • असुरत्वं (asuratvaṃ)—the might
  • महत् (mahat)—great
  • एकं (ekaṃ)—extraordinary

p. 318

भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Indra, the supporter of the whole world and our lord, dwells like a friend who wishes us well in the firmament nearest to this earth. The valiant Maruts go in front of him in battle and dwell in his own house. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

English translation (H. H. Wilson)

Our king, the nourisher of all, abides (in the firmament) nearest to this earth like a benevolent friend : the valiant (Maruts) precede him (when abroad), and dwell in his mansion : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

विश्वध्वायाः नः राजा इमां पृथिवीं च उप क्षेति (viśvadhvāyāḥ naḥ rājā imāṃ pṛthivīṃ ca upa kṣeti): the meaning is explained as follows. Indra, who supports and nourishes the whole universe, or who enjoys everything, is king and protector for us, the sacrificers, and dwells close to earth and the firmament. For this, the illustration हितमित्रो न (hitamitro na) is given: just as a friend who counsels one's welfare always lives nearby, so Indra, staying near earth and the firmament, is described as one who thinks of our good.

वीराः (vīrāḥ): the able Maruts, helpers in battle. Although the word "vīra" is conventionally used in the sense of "hero", here it is used in the sense that the Marut deities are heroes and help Indra in times of battle.

पुरसदः शर्मसदो न (purasadaḥ śarmasado na): these Maruts are those who go in front of Indra in battle and who also dwell in Indra's house; they are present wherever he is. The meaning is explained thus: the Maruts stay in front of Indra and help in times of battle, and they dwell in all the places where Indra is. The particle "na" is stated to have the sense of comparison and also the sense of prohibition (Ni. 1-4); here that particle is given the sense of the particle "ca", that of combination.

p. 319

Ṛk 22

॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

नि॒ष्पिद्व॑रीस्त॒ ओष॑धीरु॒तापो॑ र॒यिं त॑ इंद्र पृथि॒वी बि॑भर्ति ।
सखा॑यस्ते वाम॒भाजः॑ स्याम म॒हद्दे॒वाना॑मसुर॒त्वमेकं॑ ॥

niṣpidvarīsta oṣadhīrutāpo rayiṃ ta iṃdra pṛthivī bibharti |
sakhāyaste vāmabhājaḥ syāma mahaddevānāmasuratvamekaṃ ‖

॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

निःसिध्वरीः । ते । ओषधीः । उत । आपः । रयिं । ते । इंद्र । पृथिवी । बिभर्ति ।
सखायः ते । वामभाजः । स्याम । महत् । देवानां । असुरत्वं । एकं ॥ २२ ॥

niḥsidhvarīḥ | te | oṣadhīḥ | uta | āpaḥ | rayiṃ | te | iṃdra | pṛthivī | bibharti |
sakhāyaḥ te | vāmabhājaḥ | syāma | mahat | devānāṃ | asuratvaṃ | ekaṃ ‖ 22 ‖

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

हे पर्जनात्मककेंद्र ओषधीरोषधयस्ते निष्पिध्वरीर्निष्पिध्वयो नितरां त्वत्कर्तृकसिद्धिमत्यः । उतापि च आपस्त्वत्तो निःसृताः । पृथिवी ते तव भोगयोग्यं रयिं धनं बिभर्ति । पुरू वसूनि पृथिवी बिभर्ति । ऋग्वे. ३-५१-५ । इति हि निगमः । ततस्ते तव सखायो हविष्पदा नोपकारकाः स्तोतारो वयं वामभाजः स्याम। सर्वॆ वननीयधनभागिनो भवेम । तदेतद्देवानां महदैश्वर्यं ॥ निष्पिध्वरीः । षिधु संरादौ । संपदादिलक्षणो भावे क्विप् । तदस्यास्तित्यर्थे छंदसीवनिपाविति वनिप् । वनो र चेति जीप् रेफश्च । निसा सह समासः । निसः सकारं छांदसत्वादनादृत्योपसर्गात्सुनोतीत्यादिना षत्वं । जीपः पित्त्वा दनुदात्तत्वे धातुस्करः । बिभर्ति। डुभृञ् धारणपोषणयोरित्यस्य लटि बृञामिदित्यभ्यासस्यॆत्वं । निघातः । वामभाजः । भज सेवायां । भजो ण्वैः । पा ३-२-६२ । इति ण्वैः । कृदुत्तरपदस्वरः ॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

O Indra, in the form of Parjanya (the rain-god): the plants (ओषधीः (oṣadhīḥ)) are निष्पिध्वरीः (niṣpidhvarīḥ), that is, brought fully to perfection through you; and the waters also flow forth from you. The earth bears for you wealth fit for your enjoyment; Sāyaṇa cites the Nigama "Earth bears abundant treasures" (Ṛgve. 3-51-5). Therefore we, your friends and praisers who help you with offerings, would be वामभाजः (vāmabhājaḥ), sharers of all desirable wealth. That is the great lordship of the gods. NOTE

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • इंद्र (iṃdra)—O Indra, who are of the nature of Parjanya
  • ओषधीः (oṣadhīḥ)—all the plants also
  • ते (te)—by you alone
  • निष्पिध्वरीः (niṣpidhvarīḥ)—obtain nourishment and fullness of sap
  • उत (uta)—and
  • आपः (āpaḥ)—the waters also flow forth from you alone
  • पृथिवी (pṛthivī)—the earth
  • ते (te)—for you
  • रयिं (rayiṃ)—wealth
  • बिभर्ति (bibharti)—has borne
  • ते (te)—to you
  • सखायः (sakhāyaḥ)—we, who are your friends
  • नामभाजः स्याम (nāmabhājaḥ syāma)—may we enjoy all these riches NOTE
  • देवानां (devānāṃ)—of the gods
  • असुरत्वं (asuratvaṃ)—the might
  • महत् (mahat)—is great
  • एकं (ekaṃ)—and unique
भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, of the nature of Parjanya, all the plants also receive nourishment and fullness of sap from you alone. The waters flow forth from you alone. The earth has borne wealth for you. May we, your friends, enjoy all this wealth. The might of the gods is great and unique. NOTE

p. 320

English translation (H. H. Wilson)

The plants, Indra, come to perfection by you : from you the waters (flow) ; earth bears her treasures for you : may we, your friends, be sharers of these blessings : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

Addressing him with the word Indra, it is described that Indra, being the giver of rain to the worlds, performs the acts of producing, nourishing and increasing everything, and is therefore of the nature of Parjanya.

सखायः वामभाजः स्याम (sakhāyaḥ vāmabhājaḥ syāma): we, the helpers and praisers by the offering of oblations, would all be sharers of desirable wealth. It is described that the sacrificers wish Indra's welfare by offering oblations to him and by praising him; it is further explained that these sacrificers hope to obtain from Indra the wealth that is necessary for performing sacrifices and the like, and that the great might of the gods is chief and unequalled.

Closing verse and colophon: वेदार्थस्य प्रकाशेन तमो हार्दं निवारयन् । पुमर्थांश्च तुरो देयाद्विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरः ॥ (vedārthasya prakāśena tamo hārdaṃ nivārayan | pumarthāṃśca turo deyādvidyātīrthamaheśvaraḥ ‖) इति श्रीमद्राजाधिराजपरमेश्वरवैदिकमार्गप्रवर्तकश्रीवीरबुक्क भूपालसाम्राज्यधुरंधरेण सायणाचार्येण विरचिते माधवीये वेदार्थप्रकाशे ऋक्संहिताभाष्ये तृतीयाष्टके तृतीयोऽध्यायः समाप्तः (iti śrīmadrājādhirājaparameśvaravaidikamārgapravartakaśrīvīrabukka bhūpālasāmrājyadhuraṃdhareṇa sāyaṇācāryeṇa viracite mādhavīye vedārthaprakāśe ṛksaṃhitābhāṣye tṛtīyāṣṭake tṛtīyo 'dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ) यदक्षरपदभ्रष्टं मात्राहीनं तु यद्भवेत् । तत्सर्वं क्षम्यता० देव वागीश्वर नमोऽस्तु ते (yadakṣarapadabhraṣṭaṃ mātrāhīnaṃ tu yadbhavet | tatsarvaṃ kṣamyatā0 deva vāgīśvara namo 'stu te) May there be auspiciousness. Blessing. ओं तस्यत् (oṃ tasyat). Here ends the third chapter in the third Aṣṭaka of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, with the bhāṣya of Śrī Sāyaṇa and the Kannada translation.

Om. Śrī. Obeisance to the great lord of the troops. वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानामुपक्रमे यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युस्तं नमामि गजाननं ॥ (vāgīśādyāḥ sumanasaḥ sarvārthānāmupakrame yaṃ natvā kṛtakṛtyāḥ syustaṃ namāmi gajānanaṃ ‖) यस्य निश्यसितं वेदा यो वेदेभ्योऽखिलं जगत् । निर्ममे तमहं वंदे विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरं ॥ (yasya niśyasitaṃ vedā yo vedebhyo 'khilaṃ jagat | nirmame tamahaṃ vaṃde vidyātīrthamaheśvaraṃ ‖) तृतीयाष्टकमध्यस्थः तृतीयोऽध्याय आदरात् । व्याख्यातः सायणार्यॆण चतुर्थो व्याकरिष्यते ॥ (tṛtīyāṣṭakamadhyasthaḥ tṛtīyo 'dhyāya ādarāt | vyākhyātaḥ sāyaṇāryèṇa caturtho vyākariṣyate ‖) वेदः शिवः शिवो वेदो वेदाध्यायी सदाशिवः । तस्मात्सर्वप्रयत्नेन वेदमेव सदा जपेत् ॥ (vedaḥ śivaḥ śivo vedo vedādhyāyī sadāśivaḥ | tasmātsarvaprayatnena vedameva sadā japet ‖)

Ṛgveda Saṃhitā with the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya. The fourth chapter in the third Aṣṭaka. (Sūktas 56-62 of the third Maṇḍala and Sūktas 1-4 of the fourth Maṇḍala.)

In this chapter, beginning with the 56th Sūkta of the third Maṇḍala, the third Maṇḍala ends with the 62nd Sūkta. Although the Viśvedevas are the deity of this Sūkta, the Āditya, the year and its divisions are praised. Because in many places there are no words indicating a definite meaning, and because room is left for many kinds of meanings, it is not possible to say that the seer's intention for many of the matters stated in this Sūkta is just so. Nevertheless, following the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, we have given the explanation of the meaning in accordance with Yāska's etymologies.

p. 322

Sūkta 56 (Maṇḍala 3)

The fifty-sixth Sūkta.

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

न ता मिनंतीत्यष्टर्चं तृतीयं सूक्तं विश्वामित्रस्य वाचः पुत्रस्य ना प्रजापतेरार्षं त्रैष्टुभं वैश्वदेवं । तथा चानुक्रमणिका । न ताष्टाविति। सूक्तविनियोगो लिंगादवगंतव्यः । अस्मिन्सूक्ते प्रायेणादित्यैः सह संवत्सरः स्तूयते ॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

The hymn beginning न ता मिनंति (na tā minaṃti), of eight ṛks, is the third sūkta. Its seer is Prajāpati, the son of Viśvāmitra, or Vācya, son of Vāc; the metre is Triṣṭubh and the deity the Viśvedevas. The Anukramaṇikā says न ताष्टाविति (na tāṣṭāviti). The use of the sūkta in ritual is to be understood from the indication (liṅga) of its content. In this sūkta, for the most part, the year is praised together with the Ādityas.

Anuvāda: This Sūkta beginning "na tā minanti" is the third Sūkta in the fifth anuvāka. It has eight ṛks. Its seer is Prajāpati or Vācya, the son of Viśvāmitra; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the metre is Triṣṭubh. The Anukramaṇikā says "na tāṣṭau". The use of the Sūkta is to be understood according to the meaning of the ṛks. In this Sūkta the year is for the most part praised together with the Āditya.

Om. Sūkta 56. Maṇḍala 3; Anuvāka 5; Sūkta 56. Aṣṭaka 3; Adhyāya 4; Varga 1. Number of ṛks in the Sūkta: 8. Seer: Prajāpati Vaiśvāmitra or Vācya. Deity: the Viśvedevas. Metre: Triṣṭubh.

Ṛk 1

॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

न ता मि॑नंति मा॒यिनो॒ न धीरा॑ व्र॒ता दे॒वानां॑ प्रथ॒मा ॒॑ ध्रु॒वाणि॑ ।
न रोद॑सी अ॒द्रुहा॑ वे॒द्याभि॒र्न पर्व॑ता नि॒नमे॑ तस्थि॒वांसः॑ ॥

na tā minaṃti māyino na dhīrā vratā devānāṃ prathamā
dhruvāṇi |
na rodasī adruhā vedyābhirna parvatā niname tasthivāṃsaḥ ‖

p. 323

॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

न । ता । मिनंति । मायिनः । न । धीराः । व्रता । देवानां । प्रथमा । ध्रुवाणि ।
न । रोदसी इति । अद्रुहा । वेद्याभिः । न । पर्वताः । निनमे । तसि ऽवांसः ॥ १ ॥

na | tā | minaṃti | māyinaḥ | na | dhīrāḥ | vratā | devānāṃ | prathamā | dhruvāṇi |
na | rodasī iti | adruhā | vedyābhiḥ | na | parvatāḥ | niname | tasi 'vāṃsaḥ ‖ 1 ‖

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

मायिनः कपटबुद्धुपेता असुरा देवानामिंद्रादीनां प्रथमा प्रथमानि सृष्ट्यनंतरभावीनि ध्रुवाणि स्थिराणि केनापि चालयितुमशक्यानि ता तानि लोके प्रसिद्धानि व्रता व्रतानि लोकपालनादिकर्माणि न मिनंति । न हिंसंति । तथा धीरा विद्वांसोऽपि न हिंसंति । तथाद्रुहा देवमनुष्यादिषु प्रजासु द्रोहवर्जिते रोदसी द्यावापृथिव्य वेद्याभिः स्वाश्रयतया सर्वैर्वेदनीयाभिः प्रजाभिः सहितानि कर्माणि न मिनीतः । तदेतदुपपादयति । तस्थिवांसः पृथिव्यामूर्ध्वतया स्थिताः पर्वता न निनमे । निनमनीया न भवंति । एतदुक्तं भवति । यद्देवमनुष्यादीनां द्यावापृथिव्याधारकतयावस्थापनं यच्च पर्वतादीनामुन्नततयावस्थापनं तदिदं देवानां कर्म । तन्न कोऽप्यन्यथयितुमर्हतीति ॥ मिनंति । मीज् हिंसायामित्यस्य लटि मीनातेर्निगम इति ह्रस्वः । निघातः । वेद्याभिः । वेदनमर्हंति । छंदसि चेति यत्पत्ययः । निनमे । णमु प्रह्वत्व इत्यस्य कृत्यार्थे केन्प्रत्ययः । कृत्स्वरः ॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

The मायिनः (māyinaḥ) are the asuras, endowed with a deceitful mind. The acts (व्रता (vratā)) of the gods, Indra and the rest, that is, the works such as protecting the world, are प्रथमा (prathamā), coming first after creation, and ध्रुवाणि (dhruvāṇi), firm, impossible for anyone to move, and well known in the world. These the asuras do not मिनंति (minaṃti), that is, do not injure; likewise the wise (धीरा (dhīrā)) do not injure them. Likewise रोदसी (rodasī), heaven and earth, free from hostility (अद्रुहा (adruhā)) toward the beings of gods, men and the rest, do not injure the works together with the beings, वेद्याभिः (vedyābhiḥ), who are known to all through their dependence on them. He substantiates this: the mountains (पर्वता (parvatā)) standing (तस्थिवांसः (tasthivāṃsaḥ)) high on the earth are not निनमे (niname), they are not to be bowed down. What is meant: the establishing of gods, men and the rest as the supporters of heaven and earth, and the setting up of mountains and the like as lofty, are the works of the gods; no one is able to alter them.

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • मायिनः (māyinaḥ)—the deceitful asuras
  • देवानां (devānāṃ)—of the gods, Indra and others
  • प्रथमा (prathamā)—most ancient and chief
  • ध्रुवाणि (dhruvāṇi)—firm
  • ता (tā)—and well-known
  • व्रता (vratā)—acts such as protecting the world
  • न मिनंति (na minaṃti)—cannot injure and obstruct
  • धीराः (dhīrāḥ)—even the wise and discerning
  • न (मिनंति) (na (minaṃti))—cannot injure
  • अद्रुहा (adruhā)—free from hostility
  • रोदसी (rodasī)—heaven and earth also
  • वेद्याभिः (vedyābhiḥ)—together with their communities of beings, evident to all
  • न (मिनीतः) (na (minītaḥ))—cannot injure
  • तस्थिवांसः (tasthivāṃsaḥ)—firmly established
  • पर्वताः (parvatāḥ)—mountains
  • न निनमे (na niname)—(because they are established by Indra and the others) no one can lower their loftiness
भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Neither the deceitful asuras nor the wise and discerning can injure and obstruct the most ancient, firm and well-known acts of the gods, such as protecting the world. Even heaven and earth, free from hostility, cannot obstruct them. The loftiness of the mountains and the like, set high upon the earth, is also the work of Indra and the others, so no one can lower them.

p. 324

English translation (H. H. Wilson)

Neither the deceptive nor the resolute interrupt the primitive and permanent operations of the gods, nor do the innocuous heaven and earth (interrupt them), nor are the mountains standing (on the earth) to be bowed down.

विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

The power of the works of Indra and the others, such as protecting the world, is the matter of this mantra. The affairs of the universe go on in accordance with the law of the seasons (ṛtu-dharma). All activities that proceed in conformity with and in support of this rule are called vrata. The breaking of this vrata of Indra and the others cannot be effected by anyone. However deceitful and powerful the asuras may be, they cannot break these vratas. The wise and steadfast follow this same vrata, so no breach arises from them either. Therefore the affairs of the universe proceed in order just as was resolved before creation; thus the steadiness of the cosmic order is praised.

The cosmic order can be broken by two kinds of power. It may be attempted by demonic power, which hates divine culture and acts with deceit to gain selfish ends. Or poets who are filled with divine power itself, who are wise, and who can independently produce creation in accordance with Brahma's creation, may be able to break it. But there is ample basis for saying that in the affairs of the universe divine power has greater strength than demonic power. Therefore the breaking of the vrata of Indra and the others is not possible for the asuras or persons with demonic power; and since the steadfast poets and the wise have resolved to promote divine culture itself, they too cannot break this law. This is what is suggested in this mantra.

मायिनः (māyinaḥ): this word is explained as the asuras endowed with a deceitful mind. The word māyā is used in many places in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā to denote an extraordinary special power. There are contexts in which it also means an independent creative power. The epithet here denotes the creative power of the gods Indra and the others. Therefore, to understand the purport of the word in the present place, one must know in what contexts the word is used elsewhere in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā.

Broadly it can be said that this word is used in four main senses: as divine creative power, as merely physical power, as stratagem, or as the art of magic (indrajāla). It can be said to be derived from the root माज् माने (māj māne) NOTE, which has the sense of creation.

p. 325

"Māyā means prajñā (intelligence)": मायेति प्रज्ञानाम । माया, वयुनं इति तन्नामसु पाठात् । (नि. ३-१३) (māyeti prajñānāma | māyā, vayunaṃ iti tannāmasu pāṭhāt | (ni. 3-13)) Thus the Nirukta-writers have explained this word as prajñā. Citing the Ṛks मायामू तु यज्ञियानां (māyāmū tu yajñiyānāṃ) (10-88-6) and शुक्रं ते अन्यद्यजतं ते (śukraṃ te anyadyajataṃ te) (6-58-1), the appropriateness of taking the word as prajñā there was explained earlier (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Part 11, p. 514).

रूपंरूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव तदस्य रूपं प्रतिचक्षणाय । इंद्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश ॥ (rūpaṃrūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tadasya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya | iṃdro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hyasya harayaḥ śatā daśa ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-18)

This well-known mantra describes Indra's power of māyā. It is also recited in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. Sāyaṇa explains this mantra in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā in two ways. First: मायाभिः—ज्ञानमेतत् । ज्ञानैः । आत्मीयैः संकल्पैः (māyābhiḥ—jñānametat | jñānaiḥ | ātmīyaiḥ saṃkalpaiḥ)—by cognitions that are of the nature of his own resolves Indra took on manifold forms. Second: इदि परमैश्वरै इत्यस्य धातोरर्थानुगमात् इंद्रः परमात्मा । स चाकाशवत् सर्वगतः सदानंदरूपः (idi paramaiśvarai ityasya dhātorarthānugamāt iṃdraḥ paramātmā | sa cākāśavat sarvagataḥ sadānaṃdarūpaḥ)—the word Indra is formed from the root id, which gives the sense "lord of the whole universe"; therefore Indra here means the Supreme Self. He explains that the all-pervading Supreme Person is transformed, by his powers of māyā, into the form of the world beginning with ether. In both constructions the word māyā is taken as creative power. Moreover, Śaṅkarācārya too explains this mantra in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka in two ways: first प्रज्ञाभिः (prajñābhiḥ), by intelligences that effect creation; second नामरूपभूतकृतमिथ्याभिमानैर्वा (nāmarūpabhūtakṛtamithyābhimānairvā), that is, by powers of imagining such as "I" and "form". Here too the purport of the word is creative power. Power of imagination means mental creation. Mental creation may lack physical reality, but creative power must be present. For both kinds of power the synonym māyā is used in many places. Likewise:

माया वां मित्रावरुणा दिवि श्रिता सूरो ज्योतिश्चरति चित्रमायुधं । तमभ्रेण वृष्ट्या गूहथो दिवि पर्जन्य द्रप्सा मधुमंत ईरते ॥ (māyā vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā divi śritā sūro jyotiścarati citramāyudhaṃ | tamabhreṇa vṛṣṭyā gūhatho divi parjanya drapsā madhumaṃta īrate ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-63-4)

In all such places the extraordinary intelligence and creative power of Mitra and Varuṇa are described. Likewise, in the previously cited mantras such as मही मित्रस्य वरुण्य माया (mahī mitrasya varuṇya māyā) there is no room for the sense "ignorance" for māyā. In पूर्वापरं चरतो माययौता (pūrvāparaṃ carato māyayautā) (10-85-18) it is said that the Sun and Moon travel in the atmosphere by their special power of intelligence; there is no imagination in this, it is physical truth. Therefore, as stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya and the like,

p. 326

there is no room for the sense of ignorance or imagination. This meaning becomes clear if one examines the mantra cited in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa in the Pravargya section:

पतंगमक्तमसुरस्य मायया हृदा पश्यंति मनसा विपश्चितः । समुद्रे अंतः कवयो वि चक्षते मॆरीचीनां पदमिच्छंति वेधसः (pataṃgamaktamasurasya māyayā hṛdā paśyaṃti manasā vipaścitaḥ | samudre aṃtaḥ kavayo vi cakṣate mèrīcīnāṃ padamicchaṃti vedhasaḥ) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-177-1)

There Sāyaṇa explains the word asura as the Supreme Brahman and māyā as the intelligence belonging to the Supreme Brahman. Pataṅga means the Sun. The wise realise, with the heart and a restrained mind, that is, in meditation, the Sun pervaded (aktaḥ) by the intelligence of the Supreme Brahman. Hence here too there is no room for "ignorance". Just as in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā the resolve of Indra and others is designated by the synonym māyā, so the Gītā too follows it; to show this, in the Śrī-bhāṣya, in the Antaradhikaraṇa, the Gītā sentence प्रकृतिं स्वामधिष्ठाय संभवाम्यात्ममायया (prakṛtiṃ svāmadhiṣṭhāya saṃbhavāmyātmamāyayā) (Bha. Gī. 4-6) is cited and the word māyā there is explained as intelligence in the form of the Lord's resolve. The Nirukta sentence माया वयुनं, ज्ञानं (māyā vayunaṃ, jñānaṃ) is recited there as authority. There is no need to explain here what the exact purport is of the word māyā in the Brahma-sūtra passage माया मात्रं.... (māyā mātraṃ....) and the like, nor what the source of the māyā-doctrine is in philosophical procedure, its essential meaning, how this idea grew, or the purport of the contradictory statements.

Besides creative resolve or power, the word is also used in the senses of deceit, fraud, trickery:

त्वं मायाभिरनवद्य मायिनं श्रवस्यता मनसा वृत्रमर्दयः । त्वामिन्नरो वृणते गविष्टषु त्वां विश्वासु हव्यास्विष्टिषु ॥ (tvaṃ māyābhiranavadya māyinaṃ śravasyatā manasā vṛtramardayaḥ | tvāminnaro vṛṇate gaviṣṭaṣu tvāṃ viśvāsu havyāsviṣṭiṣu ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-147-2)

Here both meanings of the word māyā are shown: the intelligent Indra destroyed the deceitful enemy. Therefore, when used of Indra and the other deities, the word means creative resolve or powerful intelligence; when used of the asuras, it means deceit or fraud. In the present Ṛk too the word is used in the sense of power. Deceitful asuras need extraordinary power to obstruct the guardian and other works of the gods. But the vrata of the gods, protectors of ṛta, is not to be broken by anyone.

Vratā: the word vrata is explained as works such as protecting the world. The meaning of the word is an act performed under a fixed rule. From this point of view, in general the word vrata

p. 327

is well known as the name for sacrifices and other rites that humans perform for the gods, to please them. Here, however, the word vrata is used for the works of Indra and others; in the present Ṛk the works of the gods are also called vrata. That is, such usages show that, as the performance of sacrifice is necessary for a human from the Vedic point of view, so works such as protecting the world are equally necessary for the gods.

In sentences such as अग्ने व्रतपते व्रतं चरिष्यामि (agne vratapate vrataṃ cariṣyāmi) (Śa. Brā. 1-1-1-2) the common relation of gods and humans to vrata is indicated. Vrata can be taken to mean yajña. But if one asks how to say which of the works a human does is yajña and which is not, one must examine a mantra in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā as the answer:

नानानं वा उ नो धियो वि व्रतानि जनानां । तक्षा रिष्टं रुतं भिषग्ब्रह्मा सुन्वंतमिच्छतींद्रायेंदो परि स्रव ॥ (nānānaṃ vā u no dhiyo vi vratāni janānāṃ | takṣā riṣṭaṃ rutaṃ bhiṣagbrahmā sunvaṃtamicchatīṃdrāyeṃdo pari srava ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-112-1)

In this mantra the many-sided works of humans are described. The vratas of people are many. Among them, the carpenter wishes to do carpentry, the physician to treat disease, the sacrificer to press soma and perform the sacrifice. That is, if each person does the occupation suited to his capacity and nature, with faith and from a sense of duty, then all the works of a human are in the form of vrata; the very life of a human is in the form of vrata. In the same way all the works that the gods do for the maintenance of the world are vrata. As a human performs sacrifices and the like for the gods' satisfaction, the gods too must supply the wealth of help suited to the human's existence and nourishment. This discharge of duty is described here as vrata. As firm as all the vratas observed according to the law of the seasons are the vratas of the gods.

Two explanations of the word vrata are given in the Nirukta: निवृत्तिकर्म वारयतीति सतः (nivṛttikarma vārayatīti sataḥ)—since it forbids improper actions, it is called vrata; or since it chooses the duty to be done, it is called vrata (वृणोतीति सतः (vṛṇotīti sataḥ) Ni. 2-12). In the explanation वृणोतीति व्रतं (vṛṇotīti vrataṃ) the duty that every individual, human or god, must observe regularly is indicated. Third: यदावृणोति शरीरं । तस्मादन्नमपि व्रतमुच्यते (yadāvṛṇoti śarīraṃ | tasmādannamapi vratamucyate) (Ni. 2-12). Because it pervades the whole body and gives it strength, food too is called vrata. The word vrata in the present Ṛk can be taken to mean food. The purport is that since the wealth of food supplied by the gods is firm, no one can harm it.

p. 328

Dhīrāḥ: धीरो धीमान् (dhīro dhīmān)—this word is read among the names of the intelligent (Ni. 3-9). In the Vedas and Upaniṣads the word is used in the sense of wise, discriminating. Since the dhīra is wise, and has qualities such as conquering fear and being fearless, remaining calm of mind even in calamity, the purport is "courageous". Citing sentences such as महांतं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति (mahāṃtaṃ vibhumātmānaṃ matvā dhīro na śocati) (Kaṭha 5-4)NOTE, the distinctive character of this word was explained earlier. Since the wise, discerning person follows the vrata of the gods, there is no violation of this cosmic order. For deceitful asuras it is not possible. Therefore the vratas of the gods are unshakable and eternal. The vrata of Varuṇa, described in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā as dhṛtavrata, is likewise described elsewhere. The nature of these vratas, which cause the world's stability and protection, is this:

अमी य ऋक्षा निहितास उच्चा नक्तं ददृश्रे कुह चिद्दिवेयुः । अदब्धानि वरुणस्य व्रतानि विचाकशच्चंद्रमा नक्तमेति ॥ (amī ya ṛkṣā nihitāsa uccā naktaṃ dadṛśre kuha ciddiveyuḥ | adabdhāni varuṇasya vratāni vicākaśaccaṃdramā naktameti ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-24-10)

The light of the stars at night and the light of the sun by day are Varuṇa's vratas. The rule of this vrata is unobstructed. Varuṇa's command is the command of the universe; no one can transgress it. Because of this inviolability Mitra and Varuṇa are described as dhṛtavrata (Ni. 8-25-2)NOTE. Likewise:

नहि त्वा शूर देवा न मर्तासो दित्संतं । भीमं न गां वारयंते ॥ (nahi tvā śūra devā na martāso ditsaṃtaṃ | bhīmaṃ na gāṃ vārayaṃte ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-8-3)

Neither gods nor humans can hinder the great, generous works of Indra. All Indra's works are in the form of vrata; therefore the purport is that they are firm and protect the world.

Ṛk 2

षड्भा॒रां एको॒ अच॑रन्बिभर्तृ॒तं वर्षि॑ष्ठ॒मुप॒ गाव॒ आगुः॑ ।
ति॒स्रो म॒हीरुप॑रास्तस्थु॒रत्या॒ गुहा॒ द्वे निहि॑ते॒ दर्श्येका॑ ॥२॥

ṣaḍbhārāṃ eko acaranbibhartṛtaṃ varṣiṣṭhamupa gāva āguḥ |
tisro mahīruparāstasthuratyā guhā dve nihite darśyekā ‖2‖

ekā ‖ 2 ‖

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

अचरन् स्थायी एकः संवत्सरः षट् षट् संख्याकान् भारान् । भ्रियते पुष्पनिकासादि येष्टिति भारा ऋतवः । तान्यसंतादीन् बिभर्ति । अवयवत्वेन धारयति । तथा ऋतं सत्यभूतं वर्षिष्टं वृद्धतरमादित्यात्मकं तमेव संवत्सरं गावो रश्मय उपागुः ! प्राप्रुवंति । किंच तस्मिन्नेव संवत्सरेऽत्या आतनशीला आगमापायिधर्मोपेतास्तिस्रो महीस्त्रयो लोका उपरा उपर्युपरि वर्तमानास्तस्थुः । तिष्ठंति । लोकत्रयमेव दर्शयति । गुहा गुहायां स्वात्मनि द्वे द्यौश्चांतरिक्षं चेत्येते निहिते । न दृश्येते । एका भूमिदर्शि । सर्वभूताधारतया दृश्यते ॥ भारान् । डुभृञ् धारणपोषणयोरित्यसा दधिकरणे घञ् । कर्षात्वतो घञ् इत्यंतोदात्तत्वं । निहिते । दधातेः कर्मणि निष्ठा । गतिरनंतर इति गतेः प्रकृतिस्वरत्वं । दर्शि । दृशिर् प्रेक्षणे । कर्मणि लुङ् चिणि चिणो लुगिति प्रत्ययस्य लुक् । वाक्यभेदादनिघातः ॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

Acaran, the one stationary year, bears six burdens (bhārāḥ); the seasons are called bhāras because from them flowers, shoots and the like are borne. It holds spring and the others as its parts. Likewise the rays (gāvaḥ) reach that same year, which is ṛta, true, the most extensive, of the nature of the Sun. Further, in that same year the three great worlds (mahīḥ), moving, subject to coming and going, stand one above another. He shows the three worlds: of these, two, heaven and atmosphere, are hidden in a cave, in the year's own self, not seen; one, the earth, is seen, since it is seen as the support of all beings.

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • अचरन् (acaran)—remaining stationary, without movement
  • एकः (ekaḥ)—the one principle in the form of the year
  • षट् भारान् (ṣaṭ bhārān)—the six burdens in the form of seasons
  • बिभर्ति (bibharti)—bears
  • ऋतं (ṛtaṃ)—that which is of the nature of truth
  • वर्षिष्ठं (varṣiṣṭhaṃ)—the Āditya-principle, eldest of all
  • गावः (gāvaḥ)—rays
  • उप आगुः (upa āguḥ)—attach themselves
  • अत्याः (atyāḥ)—moving
  • तिस्रो महीः (tisro mahīḥ)—the three worlds also
  • उपराः (uparāḥ)—one above another
  • तस्थुः (tasthuḥ)—are established
  • द्वे (dve)—(of them) both heaven and atmosphere
  • गुहा (guhā)—in a hidden, imperceptible region
  • निहिते (nihite)—are placed
  • एका (ekā)—the other, the earth
  • दर्शि (darśi)—is visible (to all)
भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The principle in the form of the year, remaining stationary without movement, bears the six burdens in the form of the seasons. The rays join the Āditya, who is of the nature of truth and the best of all. The three moving worlds are established one above another. Of them, heaven and atmosphere are placed in a hidden, imperceptible region. The other, the earth, is visible to all.

p. 330

English translation (H. H. Wilson)

One stationary (year) sustains six burthens (in the seasons); the (solar) rays spread through that true and extensive (term); three revolving spheres are severally above, two of which are placed in secret, and one is visible.

विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

This mantra describes the nature of the Āditya-principle, itself unmoving and the basis of all movements of the universe. By showing the identity of the year and Āditya, it also indicates the common nature of the seasons, parts of the year, and the rays, parts of Āditya. Or, since it says षट् भारान् बिभर्ति (ṣaṭ bhārān bibharti), "bears six burdens in the form of seasons", the seasons are said to be parts of Āditya; that is, one may say that it shows non-difference between Āditya and the year. Showing their non-difference, both teach the Prajāpati-principle. One may also say that the nature of Āditya is the nature of the year, and the nature of the year is the nature of Prajāpati. There are many authorities for this.

त्रीणि च वै शतानि षष्टिश्च संवत्सरस्याहानि तावान्तंवत्सरः संवत्सरः प्रजापतिः .... .... .... .... यं प्रजायमानं विश्वं रूपमिदमनुप्रजायते ॥ (trīṇi ca vai śatāni ṣaṣṭiśca saṃvatsarasyāhāni tāvāntaṃvatsaraḥ saṃvatsaraḥ prajāpatiḥ .... .... .... .... yaṃ prajāyamānaṃ viśvaṃ rūpamidamanuprajāyate ‖) (Ai. Brā. 2-17)

The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa says that the year, with three hundred and sixty days, twelve months and six seasons, is Prajāpati.

कालात्स्रवंति भूतानि कालाद्वृद्धिं प्रयांति च । काले चास्तं नियच्छंति कालो मूर्तिरमूर्तिमान् ॥ (kālātsravaṃti bhūtāni kālādvṛddhiṃ prayāṃti ca | kāle cāstaṃ niyacchaṃti kālo mūrtiramūrtimān ‖) (Mai. U. 6-14)

Brahman, in the form of Āditya, has two forms: the first is time, the second is non-time. The root-reality of the Āditya-principle is timeless and without kalā. The whole universe produced from Āditya is kalā-natured. From this arises the birth of creatures. Therefore the year, which is of the nature of time and of kalā, is Prajāpati; such is the explanation of the Maitrī Upaniṣad. This very idea is in the present Ṛk, अचरन् एकः षड्भारान् बिभर्ति (acaran ekaḥ ṣaḍbhārān bibharti): the root-reality itself not moving, makes the whole universe produced from it move, and itself holds that whole moving universe.

चतुर्भिः साकं नवतिं च नामभिश्चक्रं न वृत्तं व्यतीरवीविपत् । (caturbhiḥ sākaṃ navatiṃ ca nāmabhiścakraṃ na vṛttaṃ vyatīravīvipat |) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-155-6)

Grammar
  • भारान् — डुभृञ् धारणपोषणयोः इत्यस्मादधिकरणे घञ् । कर्षात्वतो घञ् इत्यंतोदात्तत्वम् ।
  • निहिते — दधातेः कर्मणि निष्ठा । गतिरनंतर इति गतेः प्रकृतिस्वरत्वम् ।
  • दर्शि — दृशिर् प्रेक्षणे । कर्मणि लुङ् । चिण् । चिणो लुगिति प्रत्ययस्य लुक् । वाक्यभेदादनिघातः ।

p. 331

तस्य नाक्षस्तप्यते भूरिभारः सनादेव न शीर्यते सनाभिः । (tasya nākṣastapyate bhūribhāraḥ sanādeva na śīryate sanābhiḥ |) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-13).

This was explained earlier (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, part 11, pp. 633-4), and the point is indicated here too. Viṣṇu, who is of the nature of Āditya, is himself unmoving. By his own impulse he makes the parts of time (the year and the rest) revolve in a ring-like circuit, like a wheel turning round its spokes. These parts number ninety-four and are separately divided. Yet he himself does not move and suffers no decay. Remaining firm, he sets the pair of day and night in motion.

But one further point must be examined here. Sāyaṇa explains एकः बिभर्ति (ekaḥ bibharti) as "the one principle, in the form of the year, bears the six seasons", and गावः वर्षिष्टं उप आगुः (gāvaḥ varṣiṣṭaṃ upa āguḥ) as "the rays went to Āditya". It must not be said, then, that this mantra teaches two principles. Here एकः (ekaḥ) also means the Āditya principle, and वर्षिष्ठं (varṣiṣṭhaṃ) too stands as an attribute of Āditya alone. So there is no ground for the doubt: if एकः (ekaḥ) means Āditya, how is षडृतून् बिभर्ति (ṣaḍṛtūn bibharti) ("he bears the six seasons") consistent? In many Śruti passages the non-difference of Āditya and the seasons is stated.

आदित्यस्त्वेव सर्व ऋतवः । यद्यैवोदेत्यथ वसंतो यदा संगवोऽथ ग्रीष्मो यदा मध्यंदिनोऽथ वर्षा यदपराह्नोऽथ शरद्य दैवास्तमेऽत्यथ हेमंतस्तस्मादु .... .... .... (ādityastveva sarva ṛtavaḥ | yadyaivodetyatha vasaṃto yadā saṃgavo 'tha grīṣmo yadā madhyaṃdino 'tha varṣā yadaparāhno 'tha śaradya daivāstame 'tyatha hemaṃtastasmādu .... .... ....) (Śa. Brā. 2-2-3-9).

Āditya alone is the essence of all the seasons, or else the cause of the seasons. When he rises, it is spring. When the time for milking the cattle arrives, it is summer. The midday time is the rainy season. When the afternoon arrives, it is autumn. When the time of setting arrives, it is winter. In this way the relation of effect and cause, and the non-difference, between the seasons and Āditya, their cause, are shown.

अत्र ह वा आसावग्र आदित्य आस तम्मतवः परिगृह्यैवात ऊर्ध्वाः स्वर्गं लोकमुपोदक्रामन्त्स एष ऋतुषु प्रतिष्ठितस्तपति । (atra ha vā āsāvagra āditya āsa tammatavaḥ parigṛhyaivāta ūrdhvāḥ svargaṃ lokamupodakrāmantsa eṣa ṛtuṣu pratiṣṭhitastapati |) (Śa. Brā. 4-2-5-9).

In the beginning Āditya had pervaded this earth. When the seasons took hold of him, he flew up with them into the atmosphere. Thereafter, firmly established in the seasons, he now shines in the atmosphere. These seasons are the limbs of the year and the chief means of understanding the nature of the year. Without knowledge of these means, the nature of the year is not understood. Just as acquaintance with a house is of no use to a man who does not know the convenient door by which to enter it, so knowledge of the year cannot be gained without acquaintance with the seasons, which are the year's doors.

p. 332

Spring and winter are the doors of this year. The year is the atmosphere, and it is also the whole universe. Therefore one who has gained knowledge of the year attains an everlasting state. [सर्वं वै संवत्सरः सर्वं वा अक्षय्यमेतेन (sarvaṃ vai saṃvatsaraḥ sarvaṃ vā akṣayyametena) Śa. Brā. 1-6-1-19].

स यश्चायं पुरुषे । यश्च सावादित्ये । स एकः । (sa yaścāyaṃ puruṣe | yaśca sāvāditye | sa ekaḥ |) (Trai. U. 2-4). NOTE

The unique supreme Person, in the supreme ether, is placed in the cave as the indweller of Āditya. He creates all effects: the ether, the year, the periods such as the solstices, the rain-wealth that accords with the seasons, the food-wealth born of rain, and so on. He then enters into these very things, and all the worlds live resting on his very nature. Śaṅkarācārya explains that he is described by यश्चासावादित्ये । स एकः (yaścāsāvāditye | sa ekaḥ) (Śa. Bhā.). NOTE Here the attribute आचरन् (ācaran) ("unmoving") of the supreme entity एकः (ekaḥ) is highly apt. Though himself unmoving, he is the cause of all the worldly activities of the moving universe, which is made to revolve through the forms of the seasons.

आनेजदेकं मनसो जवीयो (ānejadekaṃ manaso javīyo) तद्धावतोऽन्यानत्येति तिष्ठत् तस्मिन्नपो मातरिश्वा दधाति (taddhāvato 'nyānatyeti tiṣṭhat tasminnapo mātariśvā dadhāti) (Īśa. 4). NOTE

This principle, which pervades everything, is without any movement the source of all the worlds that undergo change. It is by resting on this eternal principle of the Self that Mātariśvan becomes the activity of all living beings. In him everything is woven like warp and woof.

स पर्यगाच्चुक्रमकायमव्रणं आस्नाविरग्ं शुद्धमपापविद्धं । कविर्मनीषी परिभूः स्वयंभूर्याथातथ्यतोऽर्थान् व्यदधाच्छाश्वतीभ्यः समाभ्यः ॥ (sa paryagāccukramakāyamavraṇaṃ āsnāviragṃ śuddhamapāpaviddhaṃ | kavirmanīṣī paribhūḥ svayaṃbhūryāthātathyato 'rthān vyadadhācchāśvatībhyaḥ samābhyaḥ ‖) (Ī. Ka. 8). NOTE

This principle of the Self in the form of Āditya, which remains steady without any movement of its own, has spread everywhere. Though bodiless and pure, it has divided the Prajāpati principle, which is of the nature of the year, in the manner of time. But how did this unique Self-principle come to have the name "year"? The Praśna Upaniṣad answers in this way:

संवत्सरो वै प्रजापतिः । .... .... .... .... ॥ (saṃvatsaro vai prajāpatiḥ | .... .... .... .... ‖)

पंचपादं पितरं द्वादशाकृतिं दिव आहुः परे अर्धे पुरीषिणं । अथेमे अन्य उ परे विचक्षणं सप्तचक्रे षडर आहुरर्पितं ॥ (paṃcapādaṃ pitaraṃ dvādaśākṛtiṃ diva āhuḥ pare ardhe purīṣiṇaṃ | atheme anya u pare vicakṣaṇaṃ saptacakre ṣaḍara āhurarpitaṃ ‖) (Praśna. 9-11). NOTE

p. 333

This Prajāpati, who is of the nature of the year, has five feet. For this Āditya the five seasons are like feet, and with those seasons he, himself unmoving, goes round as though on five legs. Because he has created everything, he is called the Father. He has twelve limbs in the form of the months. In the half above the heaven, that is, in the third heaven, he is the Giver of rain (पुरीषि (purīṣi)). Other knowers of time say of him that he is all-seeing, that is, omniscient. They call him the one who, as seven wheels, in the form of seven horses, in the shape of a wheel moves on without pause, with six crowbars (spokes), that is, he is of the nature of time, joined with the six seasons. Whether he is described as having five feet and twelve forms, or as being seven wheels with six spokes, the purport is the same. In whatever way, the Self of time called the year, who exists in the forms of moon and sun, is the cause of the world's activity.

This same principle of the Self is described in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad with यो वै स संवत्सरः प्रजापतिः षोडशकलः (yo vai sa saṃvatsaraḥ prajāpatiḥ ṣoḍaśakalaḥ) and so on (Bṛ. U. 1-5-15).

यतं वर्षिष्ठं गावः उप आगुः (yataṃ varṣiṣṭhaṃ gāvaḥ upa āguḥ): the purport is that the rays joined the year, which is of the nature of Āditya and is the eldest and most worthy of worship of all, or the Āditya principle, which is of the nature of the year. As is said in आदित्यो ब्रह्मेत्यादेशः (ādityo brahmetyādeśaḥ) (Chā. U. 3-19-1), Āditya is the supreme Brahman. That is why, in the Ṛk Saṃhitā:

अभि यं देव्यदिर्तिगृणाति सवं देवस्य सवितुर्जुषाणा । अभि सम्राजो वरुणो गृणंत्यभि मित्रासो अर्यमा सजोषाः ॥ (abhi yaṃ devyadirtigṛṇāti savaṃ devasya saviturjuṣāṇā | abhi samrājo varuṇo gṛṇaṃtyabhi mitrāso aryamā sajoṣāḥ ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-38-4).

Aditi praises Āditya, who is of the form of Savitṛ. Varuṇa and the other gods, the sovereigns of the whole universe, worship him. Therefore Āditya is the best of all the gods and worthy of worship; hence the attribute वर्षिष्ठं (varṣiṣṭhaṃ). Since this Āditya is the supreme principle, the attribute ऋतं (ṛtaṃ) is also given. The rays of Āditya, issuing from his excellent abode, spread water in many places for the whole world and then take it back from those same directions. By these rays Āditya has pervaded all the worlds, heaven, earth and the rest. All these rays, too, establish the connection between Āditya and all the regions of the infinitely spread universe, and so bring about unity. Thus the rays that issue from Āditya pervade the universe, then come back from all directions and join him; that the whole universe is pervaded by Āditya alone is described by the passages of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as follows:

असावादित्यो देवमधु तस्य द्यौरेव शिरश्चीनवंशोऽंतरिक्षमपूपो मरीचयः पुत्राः । (asāvādityo devamadhu tasya dyaureva śiraścīnavaṃśo 'ṃtarikṣamapūpo marīcayaḥ putrāḥ |)

p. 334

तस्य ये प्रांचो रश्मयस्ता एवास्य प्राच्यो मधुनाड्यः (tasya ye prāṃco raśmayastā evāsya prācyo madhunāḍyaḥ) (Chā. U. 3-1).

This Āditya is the honey of the gods. The heaven is the tree-stem that supports it, the atmosphere is the nest, and the rays are the offspring. The rays that spread toward the east are the honey-channels of the east. The Ṛks are the bees, and the Ṛgveda is the flower. The offerings made in the sacrifice, in the form of ghee and milk, are the drops of nectar. When the Ṛk-mantras have ripened, fame, brilliance, sense-power, virility, strength and sap arise from rites such as sacrifice. Afterwards all these sap-like fruits spread toward Āditya and join him. These are the causes of the beautiful red disc of the rising Āditya.

अथ येऽस्य दक्षिणा रश्मयस्ता एवास्य दक्षिणा मधुनाड्यो (atha ye 'sya dakṣiṇā raśmayastā evāsya dakṣiṇā madhunāḍyo) (Chā. U. 3-2).

The rays that spread toward the south: the Yajus-mantras are the bees, the Yajurveda is the flower, and the ghee and milk of the sacrificial offerings are the drops of nectar. Sap and the rest arise from this, spread again toward Āditya and join Āditya himself. These are the causes of Āditya's white form.

अथ येऽस्य प्रत्यंचो रश्मयः...सामान्येव मधुकृतस्सामवेद एव पुष्पं....एतदादित्यस्य कृष्णं रूपं ॥ अथ येऽस्कोदंचो रश्मयः.... अथर्वांगिरस एव मधुकृत इतिहासपुराणं पुष्पं !....एतदादित्यस्य परं कृष्णं रूपं । (atha ye 'sya pratyaṃco raśmayaḥ...sāmānyeva madhukṛtassāmaveda eva puṣpaṃ....etadādityasya kṛṣṇaṃ rūpaṃ ‖ atha ye 'skodaṃco raśmayaḥ.... atharvāṃgirasa eva madhukṛta itihāsapurāṇaṃ puṣpaṃ !....etadādityasya paraṃ kṛṣṇaṃ rūpaṃ |) (Bhā. U. 3-3-4). NOTE

In the flower in the form of the Sāmaveda, the bees in the form of the Sāmans create drops of nectar in the form of offerings and join them to the Sun. These are the causes of Āditya's dark form. Then, from the flower in the form of Itihāsa and Purāṇa, the bee in the form of the Atharvans creates the drop of nectar in the form of sap and the like. These join Āditya. These are the causes of Āditya's deep dark form.

In these five-fold, nectar-filled, sap-natured forms of Āditya dwell the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts and Sādhyas. They also enter the red and other colours in Āditya's rays. The

p. 335

one who knows the essence of these nectars in the form of rays, that is, the one who knows the nature of Āditya, obtains a place among the Vasus, Rudras and the rest.

स्त्रियः सतीस्ता उ मे पुंस आहुः पश्यदक्रणान्न वि चेतदंधः । कविर्यः पुत्रः स ईमा चिकेत यस्ता विजानात्स पितुष्टितासत् ॥ (striyaḥ satīstā u me puṃsa āhuḥ paśyadakraṇānna vi cetadaṃdhaḥ | kaviryaḥ putraḥ sa īmā ciketa yastā vijānātsa pituṣṭitāsat ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164 16).

In explaining this Ṛk, the nature of these rays of Āditya has been described in detail (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, part 12, p. 388). In these rays of Āditya the female nature and the male nature are mingled. When it bears the embryo in the form of water, the female form appears. When the same disperses the rain, the male form appears. When it shows the female form it is extremely attractive, and when it shows the male form it is extremely powerful. These rays of Āditya spread to the many directions of the universe and to the intermediate directions. They illumine all things, take all the things of the universe into themselves, join the Sun and lay them in his womb. For this very reason Āditya has all forms. [यत्सर्वं प्रकाशयति तेन सर्वान् प्राणान् रश्मिषु संनिधत्ते (yatsarvaṃ prakāśayati tena sarvān prāṇān raśmiṣu saṃnidhatte) Praśna. 1-6].

The same view was described earlier in Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-17 by the words वत्सं बिभ्रती गौरुदस्थात् (vatsaṃ bibhratī gaurudasthāt). The purport, explained earlier with citation of Upaniṣadic and other passages, is this: the cow in the form of a ray issues from Āditya, supplies the wealth the sacrificer needs, then lifts the sacrificer up, flies away unseen, joins Āditya and becomes merged in him. [Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, 12, p. 401].

Showing the identity of this Āditya with the year, the Taittirīya Upaniṣad teaches that the Āditya principle is the Brahman principle that contains the whole universe:

आदित्यो वा एष एतन्मंडलं तपति तत्र ता ऋचस्तदृचा मंडलग्ंस ऋचां लोकोऽथ य एष एतस्मिन्मंडलेऽर्चिर्दिप्यते तानि सामानि स साम्यां लोकोऽथ य एष एतस्मिन्मंडलेऽर्चिसि पुरुषस्तानि यजूग्ंषि स यजुषा मंडलग् स यजुषां लोकस्यॆषा त्रय्येव विद्या तपति य एषोऽंतरादित्ये हिरण्मयः पुरुषः (ādityo vā eṣa etanmaṃḍalaṃ tapati tatra tā ṛcastadṛcā maṃḍalagṃsa ṛcāṃ loko 'tha ya eṣa etasminmaṃḍale 'rcirdipyate tāni sāmāni sa sāmyāṃ loko 'tha ya eṣa etasminmaṃḍale 'rcisi puruṣastāni yajūgṃṣi sa yajuṣā maṃḍalag sa yajuṣāṃ lokasyèṣā trayyeva vidyā tapati ya eṣo 'ṃtarāditye hiraṇmayaḥ puruṣaḥ) (Śrī. U. 4-14). NOTE

This Āditya principle, which lies beyond perception, shines in the form of the Sun for the favour of the world. The mass of radiance in the Sun's form is the power of the Ṛks and their place of shining. The shining flames of the Sun are the power of the Sāmans and their place of shining. The Person who stands in the middle of this circle of light,

p. 336

as the aggregate of the Yajus-mantras, is the seat of their shining. Therefore, to realise this Person-principle fully is possible only through the practice of the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā). So the Sun's disc, the light that has issued from the disc, and the Person within this ray: these three are the self-nature of the triple Veda. The purport is that the supreme principle shines only in the threefold form. Moreover:

आदित्यो वै तेज ओजो बलं यशश्चक्षुः श्रोत्रमात्मा मनो मन्युर्मनुर्मृत्युस्सत्यो मित्रो वायुराकाशः प्राणो लोकपालः कः किं कं तथस्यमन्नममृतो जीवो विश्वः कतमः स्वयंभु ब्रह्मैतदमृत एष पुरुष एष भूतानामधिपतिर्ब्रह्मणस्सायुज्यग्ंसलोकतामाप्योत्येतासामेव देवतानाग्ं सायुज्यग्ंसार्ष्टिताग्ंसमानलोकतामाप्योति य एवं वेदेत्युपनिषत् ॥ (ādityo vai teja ojo balaṃ yaśaścakṣuḥ śrotramātmā mano manyurmanurmṛtyussatyo mitro vāyurākāśaḥ prāṇo lokapālaḥ kaḥ kiṃ kaṃ tathasyamannamamṛto jīvo viśvaḥ katamaḥ svayaṃbhu brahmaitadamṛta eṣa puruṣa eṣa bhūtānāmadhipatirbrahmaṇassāyujyagṃsalokatāmāpyotyetāsāmeva devatānāgṃ sāyujyagṃsārṣṭitāgṃsamānalokatāmāpyoti ya evaṃ vedetyupaniṣat ‖) (Trai. U. 4-15).

This Āditya principle is full of manifold glories. Whoever realises whichever aspect and worships it obtains the fruit that accords with that worship. The commentator explains: एवमादिभूतो तत्तद्भावेनानुगृह्णाति तत्तदर्थिना स एवं ज्ञात्वोपासितव्यः (evamādibhūto tattadbhāvenānugṛhṇāti tattadarthinā sa evaṃ jñātvopāsitavyaḥ).

यो यो यां यां तनुं भक्तः श्रद्धयार्चितुमिच्छति । तस्य तस्याचलां श्रद्धां तामेव विदधाम्यहं ॥ (yo yo yāṃ yāṃ tanuṃ bhaktaḥ śraddhayārcitumicchati | tasya tasyācalāṃ śraddhāṃ tāmeva vidadhāmyahaṃ ‖) (Bha. Gī. 7-21). NOTE

Whatever devotee worships whichever aspect of my special glories with devotion, to each of them I give the fruit that accords with his faith and devotion. The assurance of this Bhagavadgītā verse is also stated here, according to the commentator's view. This Āditya is the light that illumines the universe. He is the vigour that gives strength to the universe and the inner essence that gives vitality. He is the eye, fame and hearing. He is the Self in the form of resolve, and Death, the cause of the world's destruction. He is also the principle of ether in the form of the vital breath, the cause of the world's growth. He is the principle of wind, which impels the world's activity. He is the form of bliss. The world-guardians such as Indra are included within him. Truth, which pervades everything, is included in him; or else this same Person, in the form of truth, is all-pervading. Svayambhū and Prajāpati, and whatever names the principle at the root of the creation of the universe is known by, all these are the glories of this Supreme Person. The knower who knows such a supreme principle and worships it attains this sāyujya with Brahman.

घृणिः सूर्य आदित्यो न प्रभा वात्यक्षरं । मधु क्षरंति तद्रसं । सत्यं वै तद्रसमापो ज्योतीरसोऽमृतं ब्रह्म भूर्भुवः सुवरों ॥ (ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityo na prabhā vātyakṣaraṃ | madhu kṣaraṃti tadrasaṃ | satyaṃ vai tadrasamāpo jyotīraso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaroṃ ‖) (Tai. U. 4-37).

p. 337

…that is, in the passage there is a description of Savitṛ as a mass of radiance. This Savitṛ is described as ghṛṇi. Ghṛṇi means "of the nature of radiance". This Āditya-principle is to be meditated on in the form of the Praṇava. This principle is of the nature of light, NOTE, of the nature of food, and pervades the three worlds, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ and Suvaḥ. The passage describes the greatness of the Supreme Person within the Āditya: this supreme light, of the nature of Praṇava, is to be meditated on in the form of Brahman.

अत्याः (atyāḥ)—"moving", that is, having the nature of moving about; it is an epithet of तिस्रः महीः (tisraḥ mahīḥ). Above, the nature of Āditya, the immovable one and the root of the world, was described; now by the epithet अत्याः (atyāḥ) the moving worlds are described. This epithet is used in many places when things whose nature is to move constantly are described; it occurs in many places as an epithet of Agni, of Āditya and of the horse, whose nature is to go wherever they wish (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-56-1; 1-190-4). The special meaning of this word was stated earlier.

तिस्रः महीः उपराः तस्थु: (tisraḥ mahīḥ uparāḥ tasthu:)—When it is said that the three worlds stand one above another, the word mahī is taken to mean "world". The words pṛthvī and antarikṣa too give, at times, not merely the sense of a single world but a collective sense in which all three worlds are included. Therefore, even though some details about the state of the earth and the other worlds are given here on the authority of Vedic passages, it is not easy to state the meaning of the passages quoted precisely, as "this and thus". Even so, one may examine in what manner the condition of the three worlds, earth and the rest, is described in the Ṛksaṃhitā.

In the Ṛksaṃhitā the description of the earth shows its extent and pervasiveness. Epithets such as pṛthvī, urvī, mahī, uttānā, aparā point to the greatness of the earth. Though it has such extent, synonyms such as bhūmi, kṣmā, gmā, iḷā show that it is different from the atmosphere and the others, which are other than the earth.

भूम्याश्च तेजः प्रदिशस्ताभ्य एना नि वर्तय । (bhūmyāśca tejaḥ pradiśastābhya enā ni vartaya |) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-19-8)

Such descriptions of the quarters also indicate the limit of the earth. But this limit does not support a separateness of the earth. Synonyms such as rodasī, dyāvāpṛthivī, kṣoṇī tell us that the earth is necessarily and continuously connected, without a break, with the heaven. Epithets such as urvī, mahī, varā describe the all-pervasiveness of heaven and earth.

p. 338

उभे अस्मै पीपयतः समीची दिवो वृष्टिं सुभगो नाम पुष्यन् । उभा क्षयावाजयन्याति पृत्सूभावर्धौ भवतः साधू अस्मै ॥ (ubhe asmai pīpayataḥ samīcī divo vṛṣṭiṃ subhago nāma puṣyan | ubhā kṣayāvājayanyāti pṛtsūbhāvardhau bhavataḥ sādhū asmai ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-27-15)

In such places heaven and earth are compared to the two hemispheres of the universe. Ubhau ardhau bhavataḥ may be taken to mean the moving part, or the part consisting of the mortal and the immortal, or two physical hemispheres. Epithets such as samīcī, dhiṣaṇe, camvā (3-55-20) describe their shape. यो अक्षेणैव चक्रिया शचीभिः (yo akṣeṇaiva cakriyā śacībhiḥ) (10-89-4): these heaven and earth, created by Indra of great nature, are like two wheels on the two sides of an axle. Both are special manifestations of Indra's greatness.

If the earth is described by epithets such as urvī and mahī, the epithet words rocana and rocanaṃ divaḥ describe the brightness of the heavenly world. What lies between heaven and earth is the atmosphere, or the world of rajas. Thus the three worlds named in the present mantra by तिस्रः महीः (tisraḥ mahīḥ), the earth, the atmosphere and the heavenly world, are the very worlds that are described by the words uttama, madhyama and avama in Ṛks such as

यदुत्तमे मरुतो मध्यमे वा यद्वावमे सुभगासो दिवि ष्ठ । अतो नो रुद्रा उत वा स्वंस्याग्ने वित्ताद्धविषो यद्यजाम ॥ (yaduttame maruto madhyame vā yadvāvame subhagāso divi ṣṭha | ato no rudrā uta vā svaṃsyāgne vittāddhaviṣo yadyajāma ‖) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-60-6)

Although all three worlds are described in the present Ṛk, the statement गुहा द्वे निहिते दर्शेका (guhā dve nihite darśekā), that two worlds are invisible and only the earth comes within sight of the eye, is new. For,

तृतीयमस्य नकिरा दधर्षति वयश्चन पतयंतः पतत्रिणः । (tṛtīyamasya nakirā dadharṣati vayaścana patayaṃtaḥ patatriṇaḥ |) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-155-5)

Man can know only the earthly world and the atmosphere, in which Viṣṇu places two steps. No one can know the heavenly world, in which this Viṣṇu places the third step.

उभे ते विद्म रजसी पृथिव्या विष्णो देव त्वं परमस्य वित्से । (ubhe te vidma rajasī pṛthivyā viṣṇo deva tvaṃ paramasya vitse |) (7--99-1)

"O radiant Viṣṇu, no one can know your full greatness. We can know only the earth and the atmosphere pervaded by you. Only you can know your supreme third world. No one else has the capacity to know its nature." In this way, wherever the three worlds are described, it is stated that two of the worlds come within human perception and only the third is beyond man's sight.

p. 339

But in the present Ṛk alone there is this difference: both the heavenly world and the atmosphere are said to be beyond perception.

But in Tai. Saṃ. 6 1-1-1, अंतर्हितो हि देवलोको मनुष्यलोकात् (aṃtarhito hi devaloko manuṣyalokāt): that is, although the world of the gods is not seen by our eyes, it is hidden within the world of men; the world of the gods and the world of men are interwoven, one within the other. Because the human world is gross, it is visible to our sight; because the world of the gods is subtle, it is not perceptible to our outer eye. Such is the explanation.

Ṛk 3

॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

त्रि॒पा॒ज॒स्यो वृ॑ष॒भो वि॒श्वरू॑प उ॒त त्र्यु॒धा पु॑रु॒ध प्र॒जावा॑न् ।
त्र्य॒नी॒कः प॑त्यते॒ माहि॑नावा॒न्स्य रे॑तो॒धा वृ॑ष॒भः शश्व॑तीनां ॥

tripājasyo vṛṣabho viśvarūpa uta tryudhā purudha prajāvān |
tryanīkaḥ patyate māhināvānsya retodhā vṛṣabhaḥ śaśvatīnāṃ ‖

॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

त्रिपाज स्यः । वृषभः । विश्वरूपः । उत । त्रिउधा । पुरुध । प्रजावान् ।
त्रिअनीकः । पत्यते । माहिनवान् । सः । रेतोधाः । वृषभः । शश्वतीनां ॥ ३ ॥

tripāja syaḥ | vṛṣabhaḥ | viśvarūpaḥ | uta | triudhā | purudha | prajāvān |
trianīkaḥ | patyate | māhinavān | saḥ | retodhāḥ | vṛṣabhaḥ | śaśvatīnāṃ ‖ 3 ‖

॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

त्रिपाजस्यः ग्रीष्मवर्षाहेमंताख्यैस्त्रिभिर्यतुभिः पाजस्यमुरो यस्य स त्रिपाजस्यः । त्रुरस्क इत्यर्थः । उरोवचनश्च पाजस्यशब्दः । इंद्रस्य क्रोडोऽदित्यै पाजस्यं । वाज. २५-८ । इत्यश्वमेधमंत्र उरःपरतयाम्ना नात् पाजसि बले साधुरिति व्युत्पत्तेश्च सर्वेषामंगानां मध्य उरसो बलवत्वात् । वृषभः स्वावयभूते वर्षर्तावसां वर्षको विश्वरूपस्तत्तद्वृत्तसाधारणकार्यैः पुष्पविकासादिभिर्लिंगैर्नानारूप उतापि च त्रुधा । वसंतशरद्धेमंताख्यैस्त्रिभिर्यतुभिरूधो यस्य स त्रुधा । प्रजावान' । प्रकर्षण जायंत इति व्रीह्यादयः प्रजाः । पुरुष नानाप्रकारेण विद्यमानव्रीहियवादिरूपप्रजावान् । किंच त्र्यनीकस्त्रिभिरुष्णवर्षशीता-

Gist of the bhāṣya

त्रिपाजस्यः (tripājasyaḥ): he whose chest (pājasya) is formed by three seasons named Grīṣma, Varṣā and Hemanta; that is, "three-chested". The word pājasya denotes the chest; in the Aśvamedha mantra इंद्रस्य क्रोडोऽदित्यै पाजस्यं (iṃdrasya kroḍo 'dityai pājasyaṃ) (Vāj. 25-8) it is read as meaning the chest; and by derivation it is what is good in strength, since among all the limbs the chest is the strongest. वृषभः (vṛṣabhaḥ): the showerer, who rains in the rainy season, its own part. विश्वरूपः (viśvarūpaḥ): of many forms, by the signs, the effects common to each season, such as the blossoming of flowers. उत (uta): and also त्रुधा (trudhā): he whose udder is formed by the three seasons named Vasanta, Śarad and Hemanta. प्रजावान् (prajāvān): prajāḥ are rice and the like, which are born forth; puruṣa (purudha): possessing progeny in the form of rice, barley and the rest, existing in many kinds. Further, त्र्यनीकः (tryanīkaḥ): he who is endowed with three hosts (anīka), the qualities of heat, rain and cold, … ### Printed p. 340

खैरनीकैर्गुणैरुपेतो माहिनावान्महत्त्ववान् संवत्सराभिमानी देवः पत्यते । आगच्छति । वृषभः सेचनसमर्थः स संवत्सरः शश्वतीनां बह्नीनामोषधीनां पुष्पफलादिसंपत्तये रेतोधा रेतस उदकस्य धर्ता भवति ॥ त्र्युधा । बहुव्रीहेरूधसोऽनज्जित्यनज् । सर्वविधीनां छंदसि विकल्पितत्वात्पुंस्यपि भवति । ऊकारस्य ह्रस्वश्छांधसः । उत्तरपदांतोदात्तप्रकरणे त्रिचक्रादीनां छंदस्युपसंख्यानमित्युत्तर पदांतोदात्तत्वं ॥

Gist of the bhāṣya

… माहिनावान् (māhināvān): possessing greatness; the deity presiding over the year पत्यते (patyate): comes. वृषभः (vṛṣabhaḥ): able to sprinkle; that year शश्वतीनां (śaśvatīnāṃ): of the many plants, for the attainment of flowers, fruits and the like, becomes रेतोधा (retodhā): the bearer of retas, water.

प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)
  • त्रिपाजस्यः (tripājasyaḥ)—having three chests named Grīṣma, Varṣā and Hemanta
  • वृषभः (vṛṣabhaḥ)—that which pours down rain
  • विश्वरूपः (viśvarūpaḥ)—that which takes on various forms according to the differences of the seasons
  • उत (uta)—and
  • त्र्युधा (tryudhā)—having three ūdhaḥ (udder) regions in the forms of Vasanta, Śarad and Hemanta
  • पुरुध प्रजावान् (purudha prajāvān)—having progeny of many kinds, in the form of rice and the like
  • त्यनीकः (tyanīkaḥ)—endowed with three qualities, in the forms of heat, rain and cold
  • माहिनावान् (māhināvān)—having a great nature; the deity presiding over the year
  • पत्यते (patyate)—comes
  • वृषभः (vṛṣabhaḥ)—the fulfiller of desires by rain
  • सः (saḥ)—that same deity presiding over the year
  • शश्वतीनां (śaśvatīnāṃ)—to the many plants and the like
  • रेतोधाः (retodhāḥ)—the one who fills them with water
भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The deity presiding over the year, having three chest regions beginning with Grīṣma, bestowing rain, having many forms according to the differences of the seasons, having three udder regions in the forms of Vasanta and the rest, having many kinds of progeny in the form of rice and the like, endowed with the three qualities beginning with heat, and of great nature, comes. That same deity presiding over the year, the fulfiller of desires by rain, fills the many plants and the like with water.

English translation (H. H. Wilson)

The three-breasted, the showerer (of rain), the omniform, the three-uddered, the parent of multiform progeny, the possessor of magnitude, followed by three hosts (the year), advances, the vigorous impregnator of the perpetual plants-

विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In the previous mantra the principle of the year is described by षड्भारान् एको आचरन् बिभर्ति (ṣaḍbhārān eko ācaran bibharti). Ṣaḍbhāra means the six seasons. The year itself, which bears such a burden of six and, holding the three worlds under its control, carries on the business of the universe, may be called a manifestation (vibhūti) of Āditya. The nature of the parts of the year, this manifestation of Āditya, and their influence are described in the present Ṛk.

p. 341

The parts of this year, which is of the form of the seasons, are compared to the chest region and to the udder region. The chest region indicates strength, and the udder region indicates the giving of abundant food. Therefore, among the parts of the year, three set forth strength and the other three the bestowing of wealth.

त्रिपाजस्यः (tripājasyaḥ)—The word pājasya is taken to mean the chest region; the purport is "having a threefold chest region". The authors of the Nirukta have read the word pājas among the names of strength (Ni. 2-9). Therefore, realising that taking pājas to mean "strength" in accordance with the Nirukta would not fit, Sāyaṇa upheld his own meaning uras, quoted the Vājasaneyi-Saṃhitā passage इंद्रस्य क्रीडोऽदित्यै पाजस्यं (iṃdrasya krīḍo 'dityai pājasyaṃ), and stated that, as the word pājasya there is a synonym of the word uras, the meaning should be given in the same way in the present passage. In places such as अरेजेतां रोदसी पाजसा गिरा (arejetāṃ rodasī pājasā girā) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-151-1) the meaning "endowed with strength" was given earlier. In the Ṛksaṃhitā this word is used in three senses. After noting that context, one should then examine what its purport is in the present passage.

विद्युद्रथः सहसस्पुत्रो अग्निः शोचिष्केश् पृथिव्यां पाजो आश्रेत् । (vidyudrathaḥ sahasasputro agniḥ śociṣkeś pṛthivyāṃ pājo āśret |) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-14-1)

One meaning is that Agni, whose vehicle is lightning and who is full of strength, obtained brightness in the atmosphere and shone; another meaning is that he obtained strength on the earth. According to the description here, the purport may be stated as: he pervaded the atmosphere or the earth and became radiant. In अरुषस्तूपो रुशदस्य पाजः (aruṣastūpo ruśadasya pājaḥ) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-29-3), since it is said that Agni destroyed the darkness and spread his own radiance, the word pājas must be given the meaning "brilliance". Likewise in contexts such as ऊर्ध्वं मधुधा दिवि पाज : (ūrdhvaṃ madhudhā divi pāja :) (3-61-5) and कृणुष्व पाजः प्रसितिं न (kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na) (4-4-1) the meaning is a mass of brilliance. But

पाजस्वंतो न वीराः पनस्यवो रिशादसो न मर्या अभिद्यवः । (pājasvaṃto na vīrāḥ panasyavo riśādaso na maryā abhidyavaḥ |) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-27-3)

in places such as this, since it is of heroes that the passage speaks, the meaning must be given with certainty as "strength" in all of them. The qualified word त्रिपाजस्यः (tripājasyaḥ) is used in the Ṛksaṃhitā only in the present Ṛk. Here the word pājasya is taken to mean uras, "chest". Or it could be the flank. There is room too for doubt whether it is the belly (jaṭhara) or the kukṣi. This is an epithet of the year-deity…

p. 342

…Therefore, in order to decide whether it is right to say "having threefold strength", or "having a threefold belly", or "having three kinds of flank", one must understand in what manner the epithets त्रिपाजस्यः (tripājasyaḥ), त्र्युधा (tryudhā), त्र्यनीकः (tryanīkaḥ) and the like describe the nature of the divisions of the year.

The epithets त्रिपाजस्यः (tripājasyaḥ) and त्र्युधा (tryudhā) indicate the six divisions of the year; त्रैनीकः (trainīkaḥ) indicates the three qualities of the year. According to the divisions now in use these three qualities fit in order.
